title: Factorio Friday Facts #300, team's favourite parts
label: developer
claim: Kozelek: 'the mini-game of trying to fit the production lines into limited, usually uneven area'. Kovarik: progression 'when old improvised parts of the factory are replaced by specialized and better organized high-production facilities'. Mason: 'the ability the game has to induce a state of flow'. Pavelcik likes that he 'alone owns any failures'. Majerech was drawn in because 'focusing on my base was exactly what I was supposed to do' rather than fighting. Norvaisas: 'finding a better or more compact way to build something'.

title: Factorio Friday Facts #309, Controversial opinions (Twinsen)
label: developer
claim: 'It's a very precise game'; 'everything can be calculated to the last item'; 'more fun to make your own setups'; importing big blueprints 'eliminates the satisfaction you feel after finishing your creation' and 'could easily make a 100-hour game into an 10-hour game'; a vanilla skip-ahead is compared to a 'level up button' in an RPG; the dev's job is to 'incentivise the player to play the game properly'. Personal opinions, post says none will be implemented.

title: Software Engineering Daily 1762, Factorio with Michal Kovarik (transcript)
label: developer
claim: 'it's always fun above realism'; 'improve the density of fun'; the core choice is 'whether investment helps you the most to move forward' (what to automate, what to do by hand); optimization is build bigger, find the slowest component, fix it, repeat; 'it feels really nice to just sit down and look at it'; planets judged by 'how many new mechanics you have compared to how many times you do those things you already know'; 'it's just repetitive and boring' when each planet repeats. Transcript says nothing on fail states or throughput as score.

title: Factorio Friday Facts #373, Space Age
label: developer
claim: Each new planet 'has its own unique theme, resource, challenges and gameplay mechanics'; goal of finishing in under 80 hours for an experienced player; 'the game was a little bit too slow and grindy, so we were speeding things up, which doesn't mean dumbing it down'; challenges 'never get too extreme'.

title: Heise interview with Satisfactory developers
label: developer
claim: Gunst: 'You're in control. You can stop at any time. You can make mistakes and no one will shout at you.' Stroebel: 'Why should we penalize players for being creative and making mistakes? Instead, we want to reward players for experimenting.' Players 'work through [their] checklist'; 'it's always fun to watch the numbers get bigger.' Nothing on optimization puzzles.

title: Game Developer: interview with the maker of (the) Gnorp Apologue
label: developer
claim: Upgrades are 'Not mandatory', 'Changes the behavior of the gnorp it upgrades', 'Works in tandem with talents to enable something new'; ideal talent offers 'a nice bonus and, at the same time, allow you to create an interesting combination' and the dev admits 'didn't hit that mark on all talents'; wants 'approachable layers where the complexity is derived from the interaction between the layers'; rejected a multiplier tied to upgrades bought because it 'would incentivize the player to buy every single upgrade, even if they did not need it'; removed a player character because it 'stands in the way of the enjoyment players derive from watching numbers grow'.

title: IncrementalDB interview with Hevipelle (Antimatter Dimensions)
label: developer
claim: 'challenges were inspired by Idle Wizard'; automation ideas from Transport Defender; proud of Reality for 'plenty of choices to make and variance between player experiences'; admits the opening is a 'click the green button -simulator'. Interview says nothing on autobuyer tuning.

title: Antimatter Dimensions wiki, Challenges
label: practitioner
claim: Challenges are modified runs of a reset layer entered at will; Normal Challenges unlock and improve the basic autobuyers; Infinity and Eternity challenges reward bonuses to earlier mechanics; Eternity challenges can be completed up to 5 times for a stronger reward. Page is a stub; design intent not stated.

title: Spiel et al., 'It Started as a Joke': On the Design of Idle Games, CHI PLAY 2019 (read as PDF text)
label: research
claim: Interviews with six idle-game designers (thematic analysis, indie-weighted). Idle games are 'explorative systems': options for 'a range of exploratory decisions and tweaks regarding local and global optimisation' with 'little consequences of failure'. Lantz on Kittens Game: 'layering on of new systems... understanding how this new system fits into the existing economy... should change my decision making'; Lantz: the world 'invites you to think and to analyse and understand the systems... in order to optimise them'. Guidelines: intertwine system variables so different decisions give different states; let players disengage at any point without substantial consequences; a sub-optimal allocation can recover through time; UIs that show the effect of a change without making it (Kittens tooltips) are player safety. Designers want an ending that says 'it's okay, you can stop playing now'.

title: Buergi, Idle Games: A Cozy Genre Turned Exploitative, Replay 2024 (read as PDF text)
label: research
claim: Secondary review. Citing Alharthi et al 2018: 'the absence of a game-over condition is considered a fundamental pillar of the genre'; sub-optimal choices cost little because 'almost any action performed by the player will lead to a boost'; working out the optimal action is 'difficult for players due to the large number of variables'; impatience drives premature spends. Argues idle games are cozy, comfort, safety.

title: Demaine et al., Cookie Clicker, Graphs and Combinatorics 2020
label: research
claim: Optimal purchase order in the Cookie Clicker model: fixed-cost case solved by dynamic programming, increasing-cost case approximated by greedy, discrete-time version strongly NP-hard. Abstract-level only; used to say the pure buy-order problem has a simple greedy near-optimum, inference.

title: IncrementalDB review of Idle Awakening: Mage's Path
label: opinion
claim: 'I've got to praise the game's automation, which is powerful, flexible and relatively simple'; 'action lists and gathering lists let you mix and match different actions'; 'at its best as you're rolling through the first few days or weeks'; 'there's also no real sense of what to progress aside from aiming at the next unlock down the line'; 'drift into tedium as everything hits diminishing returns'; 'you can only spec into one guild at a time' (single reviewer).

Player comments, unnamed.

title: IncrementalDB review of Idle Loops

Single reviewer.

title: Machinations, How to design idle games
label: practitioner
claim: 'it is important that the players be given the option to make genuinely meaningful choices'; the meta loop is 'what keeps players playing beyond the simple thrill of watching numbers go up'; use 'multiple interacting mechanics' so players keep changing strategy. Says nothing on dominant strategies.

title: thepaperpilot, Guide to Incrementals: appeal to gamers
label: practitioner
claim: Incrementals inherit strategy games' appeal of finding 'a good solution to a puzzle'; players impose their own challenges (roguelikes without meta-progression); gameplay 'paradigm shifts' prevent stagnation; warns of extrinsic-motivation build.
